headline: Cockenoe on the Last Ebb: Fluke Stack, Sea Bass Show, Bass Go Dark
subhead: The reefs are producing daylight fluke and porgies while the stripers have punched out until sundown — here's how I'm working around it.
body_markdown:
I made the call Tuesday morning to skip the Norwalk Islands entirely until the tide turned, and it was the right one. Cockenoe Reef at first light still had two overnight boats anchored on the good rubble, and with Kings Point reading 71.6 degrees, I knew the fluke bite there would hold into the morning regardless — those fish aren't going anywhere in this heat, they're just going to feed a little slower. So I ran the back channel behind Sheffield Island, worked some porgy structure on the Cows off Stamford while I waited out the crowd, and came back to Cockenoe at 10:30 when the anchor boats finally cleared for lunch. That's the chess piece you have to move on a July weekday morning on this stretch — traffic dictates timing as much as tide does.

Once I had Cockenoe to myself, the last two hours of the ebb into dead low did exactly what I expected. Fluke to 22 inches came off the drift in 18 to 24 feet, white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the edge where the reef rubble drops into sand. Keeper-class fish, not a banner day, but three in the boat with a handful of shorts thrown back is a solid morning for mid-July. We flagged last week that fluke would start sliding out of the back bays and onto the inlet mouths and ocean-facing reefs as the water warmed further — that's exactly what's happening now. The back-bay fish are thinning out and the reef bite is picking up the slack.

The Cows told a better story than I expected. Porgies are thick out there right now — 20 to 35 feet of water over that mixed rock-and-mussel bottom, bloodworms and green crab on high-low rigs, and you don't need to move much once you find the school. I sat on one drift for forty minutes and never stopped feeding fish into the box. Mixed in with the porgies were a few black sea bass pushing 15 inches, which lines up with what we called a few days back — that this fishery would keep improving into August. The hard bottom out there is holding a real resident population now, not just stragglers. If you're marking bait balls on structure anywhere from the Cows out toward Penfield Reef, drop a jig tipped with squid strip through them before you commit to anchoring — the sea bass are sitting right on the bottom edge of that structure.

Stripers are the harder conversation this week, and I'm not going to sugarcoat it. With the western Sound running warm through the mid-70s in the shallows, the bass have gone nocturnal — that's not a disappearing act, it's a thermal retreat, and it means daylight striper trips on this stretch are mostly a low-percentage play right now. I made two evening runs to Greenwich Point and worked the rock piles off the point on live bunker under a fishfinder rig, starting an hour before sunset and fishing into full dark on the last of the incoming. Both nights produced — nothing giant, schoolies to a couple of 28-inch fish, but consistent enough that I'd call it the pattern to lean on through the rest of July. Penfield Reef is holding the same story after dark: eels drifted along the reef edge on the flood, fished slow, have been the better producer than anything cast-and-retrieve.

Bluefish are the one species giving you daylight action without apology. Bunker schools have been holding tight off Greenwich Point and drifting east past the Norwalk Islands, and the blues are sitting right underneath them, same pattern we've been watching build up and down the coast. Snag a bunker on a treble, drop it back into the school, and you'll get bit — fish in the 3 to 6 pound range, plenty of blowups on top when the bait gets nervous around midday. If you want top-water action without babysitting a bass tide window, this is your play right now.

Tide-wise, we're easing toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which means softer current stages through the weekend — good news for anyone working slower presentations on the reefs, tougher news if you like a hard-running rip to concentrate bait. I'd expect the fluke and porgy bite to hold steady on Cockenoe and the Cows through this stretch since that pattern doesn't depend on a screaming tide, just clean structure and patience. For bass, I'm sticking with the last two hours of dark on the flood, working Greenwich Point and Penfield Reef with bunker and eels, and I wouldn't bother burning gas chasing daylight fish in the shallow coves right now — the water's too warm and they know it.

If the weekend boat traffic gets ugly around the islands, which it will, push east toward Penfield or stay tucked in behind Sheffield until the recreational fleet thins out midafternoon. That's the move I'd make, and it's the one I'm making again this weekend.
